title: The third meal
hook: a slow meal at dusk, with quiet songs as the day fades

segments.voice: Yesterday, menuchah, Shabbat afternoon: a nap, a walk, one sixtieth of the world to come. Your line was a taste of what's coming. Did you take the nap? Day one hundred seven.

You know how the last hour of a good vacation feels. The bags are packed. The light is going gold. Part of you is already back at work, answering email in your head. And part of you wants to hold on to every last minute. Late on Saturday afternoon, as the sun goes down, Shabbat reaches that hour. And instead of rushing to the end, many Jews sit down to eat. Again. A small meal, in fading light, with songs that get slower and quieter as the room gets darker. Today: seudah shlishit, the third meal.
screen: `THE LAST HOUR OF A VACATION.` → `THE LIGHT GOES GOLD.` → `SIT DOWN TO EAT, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Seudah means meal and shlishit means third. Friday night dinner is the first Shabbat meal, Saturday lunch is the second, and this is the third. Where does a third meal come from? Back to the manna. When Moses told the people about the first Shabbat, he said, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Eat that to-day; for to-day is a sabbath unto the LORD; to-day ye shall not find it in the field." The rabbis counted: today, today, today. Three times. So, three meals. The third doesn't have to be big. Some people have challah and a little fish or salad. In many communities it happens in the synagogue between the afternoon and evening prayers, at long tables, with the lights low or off. And it's the songs people remember. Slow, longing songs. Some sing the Twenty-third Psalm, the LORD is my shepherd. Many sing Yedid Nefesh, beloved of the soul, a love poem to God written in the sixteenth century by a Kabbalist in the town of Safed. Hasidic Jews call this hour a time of special closeness, the favor of favors, when the day's holiness is at its fullest just before it leaves. There's often no talking between the songs. People hum. Someone starts a tune, and it goes around the table again and again. The whole meal is a way of saying: we know it's ending, and we're not going to hurry it along. You stay at the table until you really can't see.
screen: `SEUDAH SHLISHIT: THE THIRD MEAL.` · `TODAY, TODAY, TODAY.` · `SLOW SONGS IN FADING LIGHT.` · `THE FAVOR OF FAVORS.` · then, large: `DON'T HURRY IT ALONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat one meal slowly at dusk. Plan it now. Settle, and breathe. Picture this evening, as the light starts to fade. Picture something simple on a plate. Picture yourself sitting down with no screen, maybe with someone, maybe alone. The first bite, slowly. Notice the light changing on the wall. Hum something, if you like. When the food's gone, stay a minute more, until it's really dark. The bell holds the time.
Seudah shlishit. The third meal: a small, slow meal at dusk on Shabbat, with quiet songs as the day fades.
Your line: don't rush the ending. Today, when something good is ending, a visit, a call, a day off, stay with it for one minute longer than you usually would. Day one hundred seven.

original.note: Hebrew: the third meal. Hasidim also call it raava d'raavin, the favor of favors, in Aramaic.

trapdoor: what you thought: an extra snack.
what it means: a slow meal at dusk that holds on to Shabbat as it fades, with quiet songs of longing.
what a scholar hears: Shabbat 117b derives three meals from the three 'today's in Exodus 16:25; Yedid Nefesh is by Eleazar Azikri of Safed.

sources.quoted: Eat that to-day; for to-day is a sabbath unto the LORD; to-day ye shall not find it in the field.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 16:25 (including the hyphenated 'to-day').
Shabbat 117b: three meals from the three 'today's. Confirm.
Yedid Nefesh: Eleazar Azikri (1533–1600), Safed. Confirm.
Raava d'raavin (Zohar term for the Shabbat afternoon hour), used especially in Hasidic circles. Confirm.
Psalm 23 at the third meal is a custom in many communities. Confirm.
